places.name: Banos

visits.text: Leave Latacunga for Quilotoa Lagoon, about 2 hours west through the Andean countryside. Quilotoa is a volcano whose last confirmed eruption dates to 1280. It left behind a crater 3 km in diameter and 250 m deep, filled with turquoise-green water that changes color with the light. At 3,914 m above sea level, it's one of Ecuador's most photogenic sites. The view from the crater rim is striking. Descend to the lake if you have the energy—a steep 30-minute descent, but the climb back up (40–50 min) is exhausting at this altitude. Mules are available for the ascent for those who are too tired.

The Waterfall Route (Ruta de las Cascadas) is Baños' main attraction: nearly 20 km toward Puyo, with around sixty waterfalls along the Pastaza River valley. Rent a bike—the road is almost entirely downhill. First stop: Manto de la Novia (“bridal veil”) waterfall, which you can cross above in a tarabita over the gorge. Continue to Río Verde and Pailón del Diablo (“devil's cauldron”)—80 meters high, with enough power to soak you in 30 seconds when you're nearby. Passages cut into the rock let you walk behind the waterfall. It's one of the most impressive in South America.

On the way back to Baños, stop at Casa del Árbol, a former Tungurahua volcano observation post turned attraction. Its famous swing dangling over the void at 2,660 m delivers vertigo-inducing photos with the volcano behind — weather permitting. The site is small; budget 30 minutes.

activities.text: After Quilotoa, get back on the road to Baños de Agua Santa (3–4 hours). You descend from the highlands into the Pastaza River valley, dropping from 3,900 m to 1,815 m—the climate warms noticeably and the vegetation becomes tropical. On arrival in Baños, walk around the central square to see the Basílica de la Virgen de Agua Santa, a pilgrimage site whose frescoes recount miracles attributed to the Virgin. Then climb to the Bellavista viewpoint for a first view of the town dominated by Tungurahua volcano (5,023 m), active since 1999.

Ride the waterfall route from Baños to Río Verde by bike. The descent is easy and the scenery shifts from Andean mountains to tropical vegetation. For the return journey, local pickup trucks carry bikes and riders back up to Baños—very convenient.

At the end of the day, relax in the Baños hot springs. The hot sulfurous water comes directly from Tungurahua volcano. There are several pools at different temperatures (18–54°C). The local specialty to try on your way out is melcocha, a sugarcane candy hand-stretched in front of you.

places.name: Cuenca

visits.text: It is a long day on the road (4-5 hours) between Riobamba and Cuenca, but the detour through Ingapirca makes it fascinating. Ingapirca is about 62 km from Cuenca, a 1-hour 10-minute drive. At an altitude of 3,160 metres, you will discover Ecuador's most important archaeological site. First occupied by the Cañari people from around 500 and conquered by the Incas around 1487, it contains an elliptical Temple of the Sun - unique in the entire known Inca world. The diorite stones are fitted together without mortar with surgical precision. Charles Marie de La Condamine was the first European to describe it in 1739.

About 62 km from Cuenca, a 1-hour 10-minute drive, the guided tour of Ingapirca (compulsory and included in the ticket) lasts about 40 minutes and covers the Temple of the Sun, the agricultural terraces and a natural rock shaped like an Inca face. The museum, opened in 2018, displays ceramics, textiles and tools from both civilisations. Do not expect Machu Picchu - the site is modest in size - but the story of the Cañari-Inca fusion is captivating. If you still have energy, a 30-minute trail descends into the Intihuayco valley.

Arrive in Cuenca by late afternoon. Detour through the Turi viewpoint on the hill south of the city. From there, you'll have the best panoramic view of Cuenca and its sky-blue domes—the evening light brings out the red tile roofs and bell towers. It's the perfect postcard to open your Cuenca stay.

Start at Parque Calderón, the city's heart, and the Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción that overlooks it. Its blue domes are Cuenca's symbol—visible from everywhere. Begun in 1885 and completed only in 1975, it was supposed to have two additional towers topped with cupolas, but the architect had to abandon the plan: the ground couldn't support more weight. The interior floors are Carrara marble imported from Italy. Climb the 155 steps to the domes for a plunging view over the historic center.

Across the way, don't miss the Catedral Vieja (El Sagrario), one of Latin America's oldest churches, built in 1557. Now transformed into a religious art museum, it surprises with its pastel ceiling paintings—very different from the typical gilded church interiors. Entrance is free.

Two blocks from the cathedral, the Plaza de las Flores is enchanting. The permanent flower market, run by women in traditional dress, overflows with roses, lilies, and orchids—Ecuador is one of the world's largest flower exporters. The white Carmen de la Asunción church (1730) forms a dazzling backdrop. This plaza was voted one of the world's most beautiful flower markets.

Walk down to the Pumapungo Museum, built on the ruins of the ancient Inca city of Tomebamba—"the Puma's Gate." The open-air archaeological site shows remnants of an Inca administrative center, and the adjoining botanical garden presents over 200 native Andean plants. The indoor museum covers Ecuador's ethnographic history and indigenous cultures. Free admission.

Day trip to Cajas National Park, just 40 minutes from Cuenca toward Guayaquil. This 28,544-hectare park, created in 1977 and designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve, holds over 230 lakes of glacial origin between 3,100 and 4,450 meters elevation. The páramo landscapes—these high grassy moorlands—recall Scotland on an overcast day. A remnant of the Inca Trail crosses the park for 4 km between Luspa cave and Mamamag lake. Entrance is free but registration with passport is mandatory.

For an accessible hike, do the loop around Laguna Toreadora (trail #1, 2.2 km, ~1h30) from the visitor center. If you're in shape and acclimatized, climb toward the Lagunas Unidas on trail #4 (4.2 km) which crosses a polylepis forest—these twisted trees grow higher than any other tree on Earth. The lakes follow one another in total silence, broken only by birds. Bring warm, waterproof clothing: weather changes fast at this altitude.

activities.text: Enjoy the evening for a first meal in this city renowned for its Andean gastronomy. Mote pillo (white corn sautéed with eggs and onions) is the local specialty. The small restaurants around the market are the best. Cuenca is very pleasant on foot in the evening, the pedestrian streets are well-lit and the atmosphere is much calmer than Quito.

Late in the day, walk down Calle Larga to the Barranco neighborhood along the Tomebamba River. The colorful facades overlooking the river form one of Ecuador's most photographed landscapes. Take the opportunity to visit a Panama hat workshop—here they call them "sombrero de paja toquilla." The Cuenca region is the heart of this artisan production inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. A good hat takes weeks of weaving.

On the return from the hike, stop at the Tres Cruces viewpoint, the highest point on the Cuenca-Guayaquil road (4,167 m). On clear days, you can see the Pacific coast from this point—it's the only place in Ecuador where both slopes are visible simultaneously. Back in Cuenca, rest your legs in the Baños de Cuenca hot springs (8 km from downtown), fed by volcanic sources. Hot water at this altitude is pure luxury.

visits.text: Drive from Cuenca to Guayaquil (about 4h), a spectacular 2,500-meter descent from altitude to sea level. You'll pass through Cajas park (quick view if you skipped it yesterday) then cross banana and cacao plantations as you approach the coast. The tropical heat will hit you all at once—prepare for thermal shock after the Andes.

Arriving in Guayaquil, head straight to the Las Peñas neighborhood, the city's oldest. Climb the 444 steps of Cerro Santa Ana through the brightly painted facades—each landing bears a number and an anecdote. At the top, the lighthouse and small chapel offer a panoramic view over the Guayas River, the Malecón, and the city rooftops. Go in late afternoon for the golden light and the atmosphere of the bars and art galleries lining the stairs.

Walk down to the Malecón 2000, the 2.5-km promenade along the Guayas River. Renovated in the early 2000s, it connects the artisan market in the south to the Las Peñas neighborhood in the north. You'll find gardens, fountains, monuments, and Parque Seminario—don't miss it: its trees are populated by land iguanas basking in the sun by the dozens. Kids love them, but keep your distance: they can bite.

Drive from Montañita to Guayaquil (about 3h). Arriving, start with Parque Seminario (also called Parque de las Iguanas), right downtown. Dozens of land iguanas lounge in the trees and on the lawns—a surreal spectacle in the middle of a big city. Guayaquil's neo-Gothic cathedral borders the park. Grab a bench to watch local life between the giant lizards.

Continue to the Mercado Artesanal, Guayaquil's largest craft market. You'll find Panama hats, hammocks, tagua jewelry (vegetable ivory), and Andean textiles. Vendors are open to bargaining—but stay reasonable. The market is covered, which is appreciated when Guayaquil's heat hits hard.

If you didn't climb Cerro Santa Ana on your first pass (Day 8), now's the time. Otherwise, explore the Barrio del Astillero, a neighborhood in transformation that preserves 19th-century wooden houses. This neighborhood, the city's old shipyard, is less touristy than Las Peñas and gives a more authentic glimpse of working-class Guayaquil.

Start with the MAAC (Museo Antropológico y de Arte Contemporáneo), located at the southern end of Malecón 2000. This free museum displays a collection of over 50,000 archaeological pieces tracing 5,000 years of Ecuadorian cultures, from the Valdivia civilization (South America's oldest ceramic culture) through the colonial era. The contemporary art section is also worth a look.

If you still have a morning, cross the pedestrian bridge to Isla Santay, a nature reserve in the middle of the Guayas River. This mangrove island is accessible for free and offers 2 km of boardwalk trails over the water. You'll encounter herons, iguanas, and mangrove crabs. It's a surprising nature break just a few hundred meters from downtown.

activities.text: Evening on the Malecón: the riverside restaurants serve shrimp ceviche (Guayaquil's specialty) and encebollado, a tuna and onion soup considered the country's best hangover cure. The nighttime atmosphere is lively, especially on weekends.

End of day on the Malecón del Estero Salado, less known than Malecón 2000 but just as pleasant. This promenade follows an arm of sea bordered by mangroves right in the city center. Boats offer short sunset rides on the water. The atmosphere is more local and less touristy than the main Malecón.

Final stop before departure: the Parque Histórico de Guayaquil, located in Samborondón (20 minutes by taxi). This park-museum reconstructs 19th-century coastal architecture and houses animals in a restored mangrove setting. It's a good place to understand the coastal region's history before catching your flight from José Joaquín de Olmedo airport, 10 minutes from downtown.

visits.text: A big driving day: from Mindo, you pass back through the Pichincha foothills, then head due south to Cotopaxi National Park (allow 4–5 hours in total). Cotopaxi awaits with its almost perfect snow-covered cone at 5,897 m—one of the highest active volcanoes in the world. Its last major eruption, in 1877, sent mudflows that destroyed Latacunga and several towns in the valley. Bring warm clothes: the park is windy and you'll be above 3,800 m.

Stop at Limpiopungo Lagoon, at 3,800 m above sea level at the foot of the volcano. On clear days, Cotopaxi's snow-covered cone is reflected in the calm water—Ecuador's classic postcard image. The trail circles the lake in 1 to 1.5 hours; it's easy and ideal for spotting Andean ducks, Andean gulls, and, with luck, a carunculated caracara. Walk slowly—you'll feel the altitude.

activities.text: If you're well acclimatized, drive up to the parking lot at 4,500 m, then hike to the José Rivas refuge at 4,864 m—a steep half-hour climb through volcanic sand. From the refuge, you can continue for 45 min to the glacier's edge at 5,000 m. You're guaranteed to be short of breath, but the view over the ice cap and the Avenue of Volcanoes is breathtaking. Have a hot chocolate at the refuge on the way down.

visits.text: A long drive from Otavalo to Mindo (around 4 hours via Nanegalito). The landscape changes radically: you leave the dry highlands and plunge into the cloud forest of the Andean Chocó at 1,250 m above sea level. Mindo is a former farming village turned naturalist paradise—BirdLife International has designated it an Important Bird Area. Ecuador is home to 130 of the world's 340 hummingbird species, and many live here. On arrival, use the feeders at your accommodation to watch these little colorful rockets.

Head to the Mariposario, 2.5 km from the center. Inside an enormous glass greenhouse, over 1,000 butterflies from 25 species fly freely around you. Place a piece of banana on your fingers—they'll come to feed on it. With luck you'll see a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis. At the entrance feeders, hummingbirds put on a nonstop show.

activities.text: Ride the tarabita (a metal gondola suspended from a cable) across the canopy to reach the waterfall sanctuary. Three trails: Nambillo waterfall (15 min one way, easy), La Reina waterfall (50 min, the most impressive), or the 5-waterfall circuit (2 hours round trip). The paths are narrow and muddy—bring hiking shoes, a raincoat, and a swimsuit if you want to swim at the foot of the falls.

At the end of the day, join a chocolate-making workshop. Ecuadorian cacao (the “fino de aroma” variety) is among the world's finest, and several Mindo producers offer the complete process, from bean to bar, with a tasting included.

visits.text: Coastal drive south (about 1h) to Montañita, Ecuador's most famous surf village. The vibe is radically different from the rest of the trip: this is a concentration of backpackers, surfers, and craft vendors. The main street is pedestrian, lined with bars, ceviche restaurants, and shell jewelry shops. If you're seeking calm, continue 5 km north to Olón beach, much quieter and just as beautiful.

Before settling in Montañita, push 5 km north to Olón. This fishing village is the antithesis of Montañita: calm, family-friendly, with a huge beach nearly deserted on weekdays. On the cliff separating the two villages, the Santuario de Olón—a small white church perched above the ocean—offers a magnificent panorama of the coast. The trail leading there from the beach takes 15 minutes and is worth the detour for photos.

Back in Montañita, the beach offers a long stretch of sand with consistent waves—ideal for surfing. Schools offer lessons for all levels, budget 2h for an introduction. Walking north from the center, a wilder spot at the base of the rocky point attracts locals away from the crowds. If surfing isn't your thing, swimming is pleasant but watch the current—stay in supervised areas.

activities.text: Montañita is mostly known for its nightlife. Bars open in late afternoon with live music, and the party continues until late. If you prefer a more zen plan, sunset from the rocky point north of the beach is superb—bring a local beer and settle in. The shrimp cocktail sold by beach vendors is a classic end-of-day treat.

days_plan.itin_title: Ecuador Road Trip: Volcano Highway, Inca Ruins & Pacific Coast

visits.text: Head to Otavalo, 95 km north of Quito along the Pan-American Highway—allow 2 hours of driving with Cayambe and Imbabura volcanoes as a backdrop. On arrival, go straight to Plaza de los Ponchos, South America's most famous artisan market. Its origins trace back to pre-Columbian times, when Otavaleños were already trading textiles and foodstuffs. Open daily, it bursts into life on Saturdays with hundreds of stalls selling handwoven ponchos, alpaca wool blankets, silver jewelry, and hammocks. Bargain—it's expected and part of the game. On weekdays, prices are better and the atmosphere is more relaxed.

Walk around Parque Bolívar and along Calle Sucre. Otavalo sits at 2,530 m above sea level at the foot of Imbabura (4,630 m) and Cotacachi (4,944 m) volcanoes. Otavaleños are recognizable by their long black braids and traditional dress—a cultural pride remarkably preserved through the centuries. If you're here on a Saturday, don't miss the livestock market 1 km from the plaza, where cows, pigs, chickens, and guinea pigs change hands from 6am.

Leave early for Cuicocha Lagoon, 30 minutes from Otavalo. This crater lake formed 3,000 years ago during an eruption of Cotacachi volcano—3 km in diameter, 200 m deep, with two small islands in the middle shaped like guinea pig backs (hence the Quechua name: “guinea pig lake”). The water ranges from deep blue to emerald green. You can take a boat ride around the islands (25 min) to admire the colors up close.

On the way back, stop in Peguche village, 3 km from Otavalo. Its 18-meter waterfall is sacred to the Otavaleños—every June 21, during Inti Raymi (the Festival of the Sun), locals come to purify themselves in the cold water during nighttime ritual baths. Outside this period, it's a peaceful walk through a eucalyptus forest (20 min). The village specializes in weaving—step into a workshop to watch traditional looms in action.
Passing through Cotacachi, 20 minutes from Otavalo, stop in this small town famous for its leather crafts—jackets, bags, belts, and boots line the main street at very reasonable prices.

activities.text: At the end of the day, make a detour to Lake San Pablo, 10 km away at the foot of Imbabura volcano. Stop at the El Lechero viewpoint: the thousand-year-old tree standing there is a sacred site where indigenous people come from across the country for purification rituals. The 360° view over the lake, the volcano, and the countryside's patchwork of crops is well worth the detour.

Hike the Gorki Campuzano trail around Cuicocha Lagoon: 14 km along ridges between 3,100 and 3,500 m above sea level, with magnificent views over the crater and, on clear days, Imbabura, Cayambe, and Pichincha volcanoes. The trail is marked and hilly but has no technical difficulties. Bring water and snacks—there's nothing along the route.

places.name: Puerto Ayora

visits.text: After landing at Baltra and taking the bus then ferry to Santa Cruz, you arrive in Puerto Ayora—the most populous town in the Galápagos, with 18,000 residents. Get your bearings: the waterfront runs along Avenida Charles Darwin, and sea lions are already lounging on the public benches on the dock. Drop your bags and head to the Charles Darwin Research Station, a 20-minute walk from the center. Founded in 1959 and inaugurated in 1964, the station is where more than 150 scientists work to conserve the archipelago. Admission is free—just show your National Park ticket.

Next door, head to the Fausto Llerena Breeding Center. Since 1965, more than 2,000 giant tortoises have been raised here and then released into the wild. You'll see hatchlings measuring 8 cm and adults weighing 250 kg—the contrast is striking. This is also where Lonesome George, the last tortoise from Pinta Island, rests; he died in 2012 at over 100 years old. His embalmed body is displayed in an air-conditioned room. Allow about 45 minutes, and don't miss the botanical garden with Scalesia affinis, an endemic giant daisy.

Continue to Playa de la Estación, a short walk from the Charles Darwin Research Station. This small beach of fine sand is the most accessible spot from Puerto Ayora—15 minutes on foot from the dock. The water is clear and shallow, perfect for a first snorkeling session with marine iguanas, Sally Lightfoot crabs, and sometimes small reef sharks. Bring water sandals, as the entry is rocky.

If you still have energy, walk to Tortuga Bay—allow 30 to 45 minutes from the center along a paved trail through Opuntia cacti and palo santo trees. You arrive first at Playa Brava: a long ribbon of white sand pounded by waves, where swimming is prohibited but iguanas abound. Continue for 20 minutes to the right to reach Playa Mansa—calm, turquoise water and small blacktip sharks in the lagoon. You can rent a kayak there. Bring water and snacks; there are no shops on site. You must return before 6 pm—that's when sea turtles come to lay their eggs.

This morning, head to Santa Cruz's highlands. Take a taxi from Puerto Ayora (20 minutes; negotiate the round-trip fare). First stop: Los Gemelos, two enormous sinkholes on either side of the main road. Despite their name, “twin craters,” they are actually collapsed magma chambers—each is about 300 meters in diameter—they are not calderas but pit craters, depressions formed by collapse. Around them, the Scalesia forest—the world's largest daisy, endemic to the Galápagos—forms a dense canopy. Keep your eyes open: 8 of Darwin's 13 finch species live here, as does the vermilion flycatcher. Arrive early in the morning, when the birds are more active.

Continue to El Chato reserve, 22 km from Puerto Ayora. This 12-hectare private property is one of the few places in the world where you can get close to completely wild Chelonoidis porteri giant tortoises. They weigh up to 250 kg and measure 1.5 meters—you'll find them grazing peacefully or wallowing in muddy pools. Keep your distance (at least 2 meters), but the photos are spectacular. Rubber boots are provided if the ground is muddy.

Right next to El Chato, descend into the lava tunnels. These underground cavities formed when surface lava cooled while magma continued flowing underneath, leaving passageways you can explore for several hundred meters. Bring a headlamp (or use your phone light). The walls bear colorful mineral traces, and the acoustics are surprising. Mind your head in the low passages.

activities.text: In the evening, head down to Puerto Ayora's fish market. Fishermen cut up fresh fish on the dock while pelicans, sea lions, and herons squabble over scraps—a hilarious and very photogenic spectacle. Just behind the market, street kiosks serve grilled fish.

Back in Puerto Ayora at the end of the day, stop at Las Grietas canal. To get there, take the water taxi from the main dock, then walk for 10 minutes. It's a volcanic fissure filled with crystal-clear water between two lava walls—a shallow spot for swimming and snorkeling, provided you are accompanied by a guide.

places.name: Puerto Baquerizo Moreno

visits.text: Take the morning ferry from Isabela to San Cristóbal. Be aware: there is no direct service—you first go through Santa Cruz (approximately 2 hours 30 minutes), then take a second ferry to San Cristóbal (another 2 hours). Allow half a day of travel with the stopover in Puerto Ayora. Bear with the seasickness. San Cristóbal is an island in the archipelago (2.4 to 4 million years old), the first where Darwin set foot in 1835, and also happens to be the administrative capital of the Galápagos. Puerto Baquerizo Moreno welcomes you with sea lions sprawled everywhere—on benches, jetties, and rocks.

San Cristóbal's highlight: a boat excursion to Kicker Rock (León Dormido), 1 hour 30 minutes offshore. This eroded volcanic cone rises 148 meters above the water, split in two by a 20-meter-deep channel. From the north it looks like a shoe (hence “Kicker Rock”); from the south, a sleeping lion. Snorkeling in the channel is among the most spectacular in the Galápagos: hammerhead sharks, Galápagos sharks, whitetip sharks, green turtles, eagle rays, and schools of tropical fish. Be aware: the currents are strong; this is not a spot for beginners. Allow 6 hours for the tour, including lunch and a beach break.

Back at the harbor, visit the Interpretation Center just north of Puerto Baquerizo Moreno. Inaugurated in 1994 with Spanish development assistance, it traces the Galápagos' natural and human history—from their discovery in 1535 to the penal colonies, including Darwin's theories. Admission is free. The building is the starting point for several trails to Cerro Tijeretas and Punta Carola.

Your last morning in the archipelago—don't waste it. Set off early on foot from Puerto Baquerizo Moreno toward Cerro Tijeretas (Frigatebird Hill). The 5.5-km loop begins at the Interpretation Center. A trail paved with lava stones climbs through an arid area full of cacti, then the vegetation changes with altitude. At the summit (roughly 200 m), panoramic views take in Wreck Bay, Lobos Island offshore, and Kicker Rock in the distance. This is one of the few places where the two frigatebird species (magnificent and great) nest in the same colony. You'll also come across a World War II cannon recovered by the Ecuadorian navy.

On the way down, turn off toward Darwin Cove (Muelle Tijeretas)—a free, easy snorkeling spot sheltered between the rocks. Sea lions, sea turtles, marine iguanas, and tropical fish await. Check your surroundings carefully before jumping into the water—male sea lions can be territorial around their young.

Continue along the trail to Punta Carola, a crescent-shaped beach surrounded by volcanic rock formations, a 15-minute walk from Playa Mann. On the way, stop at the statue of Charles Darwin—a chance for a souvenir photo. The beach is popular with surfers (waves up to 3 meters at high tide), as well as sea lions that peacefully colonize it. If the swell is strong, just watch—the surrounding rocks are treacherous.

activities.text: Finish the day at Playa Mann, the beach closest to the town center—a 10-minute walk. Fine sand, clear water, and above all: sea lions everywhere. They lounge on the sand among the swimmers with complete confidence. If you're there at sunset, the light over the bay is superb.

If your flight is at the end of the day, take one final detour to La Lobería, a beach 15 minutes by taxi from the center. This is marine iguana country—you'll see dozens on the black lava rocks, expelling salt through their nostrils. The atmosphere is wild and unspoiled, perfectly capturing the magic of the Galápagos. Enjoy it one last time before heading to San Cristóbal Airport for your return flight to Guayaquil or Quito.

visits.text: Drive from Guayaquil north along the Pacific coast (about 3h). You'll follow the Ruta del Spondylus, the coastal road named after a shell sacred to pre-Columbian civilizations. The landscape shifts dramatically: tropical dry forest, giant cacti, and small fishing villages. Arrive in Puerto López, a quiet town that serves as base for exploring Machalilla National Park.

In the afternoon, head to Los Frailes Beach, considered one of the most beautiful beaches on mainland Ecuador. Located in Machalilla National Park, it forms a crescent of white sand edged by cliffs and turquoise water. You can drive to the car park near the beach or walk along a trail through the dry forest (free, with compulsory registration at the park entrance). There are no facilities on the beach - bring water and a picnic. It is completely peaceful on weekdays.

Full day on Isla de la Plata, nicknamed "the poor man's Galápagos"—a somewhat reductive nickname but it gives the idea. This island located about 40 km offshore from Puerto López hosts colonies of blue-footed boobies, frigatebirds, and albatrosses (April to November for the latter). The boat crossing takes 1h30 and can be rough—take motion sickness medication if you're prone.

On the island, two guided hiking trails (mandatory) of about 2h take you through blue-footed booby nests. These birds have no fear of humans and you can observe them from a few meters away—their mating display, where the male lifts his blue feet one at a time, is hilarious. After the hike, a snorkeling session is included in the excursion: sea turtles, rays, and tropical fish populate the waters around the island.

activities.text: If you're traveling between June and September, watch for humpback whales from Puerto López's waterfront. They migrate each year from Antarctica to breed in the warm waters off Ecuador's coast. Boat tours leave every morning from the port—book the day before. The sight of these 15-meter giants breaching is stunning.

Back at port by mid-afternoon, enjoy Puerto López's waterfront for fresh ceviche prepared by fishermen. The colorful boats on the beach, pelicans circling the stalls—the atmosphere is authentic and relaxed. Pacific sunset guaranteed.

visits.text: Take an early morning ferry from Puerto Ayora—allow about 2.5 hours for the crossing, which is often rough. Bring seasickness tablets. On arrival in Puerto Villamil on Isabela, you discover a fishing village of 2,200 inhabitants, much quieter than Puerto Ayora. Drop your bags and cycle toward the Wall of Tears. The trail follows the coast for 5 km from the village—sand, then gravel; allow 1 hour by bike.

The Muro de las Lágrimas is a wall of volcanic stones, 5 to 7 meters high depending on the section, 3 meters wide and more than 100 meters long, built between 1946 and 1959 by prisoners of a penal colony. President Velasco Ibarra established this prison on the island in 1945, a natural jail surrounded by 1,000 km of shark-infested ocean. The construction served no useful purpose: it was forced labor intended to break the inmates. Locals say the wall is haunted and groans can be heard at dusk. Climb the steps to the viewpoint at the top for a magnificent view over Isabela.

On the way back, stop at the wetlands to watch flamingos—the largest colony in the Galápagos is here, in the lagoons along the trail. The best time is between 6am and 9am, when they are actively feeding. You'll also pass through a natural mangrove tunnel harboring the archipelago's 4 endemic species.

The highlight of your time on Isabela—and probably of the entire trip. In the morning, take a boat to Los Túneles (Cabo Rosa), 1 hour from Puerto Villamil. These submerged lava tunnels formed millions of years ago when lava flows met the ocean: the outer layer solidified while magma continued flowing inside, leaving a labyrinth of arches, bridges, and natural pools. Access is tightly regulated—the National Park limits the number of boats and visitors each day. Book the day before through an agency; a naturalist guide is mandatory.

Snorkeling in the tunnels is exceptional: the water is turquoise, calm, and shallow (2 to 10 meters). You'll see whitetip sharks asleep on the bottom, enormous green turtles (up to 2 meters across), rays (eagle, golden, manta), and, with a little luck, Pacific seahorses—Los Túneles is one of the few places in the world where they are easy to observe. On land, climb onto the lava arches to watch blue-footed boobies—you may see their courtship dance.

activities.text: At the end of the day, head to Concha de Perla, a small natural lagoon accessible by a wooden boardwalk from Puerto Villamil's port. It's Isabela's easiest free snorkeling spot: calm, shallow water, where you'll swim with sea lions, sea turtles, rays, and schools of tropical fish. No guide required. Bring your mask and fins—you can also rent them in town.

In the afternoon, set out on the Sierra Negra volcano hike, the only one of Isabela's 5 volcanoes open to visitors. Its caldera is 10 km wide and 300 m deep. The trail is about 16 km round trip from the starting point (21 km from Puerto Villamil by taxi), with 200 m of elevation gain: allow 5 to 6 hours. You first climb through a humid forest, then the landscape changes radically: black lava fields, fumaroles and ash cones. The last eruption was in 2018, so you will walk on relatively recent lava. Bring water, sunscreen, a waterproof jacket and good shoes. A guide is mandatory. Note: combining Los Túneles and Sierra Negra on the same day is very ambitious. In practice, the hike starts early in the morning (6–7am), as does the Los Túneles tour. If you must choose, Los Túneles is Isabela's most unique experience; plan Sierra Negra for a possible third day.

places.name: Quito

visits.text: Start at Plaza Grande, the beating heart of the historic center listed by UNESCO since 1978. Around you are the Palacio de Carondelet (the presidential residence since the 16th century), the metropolitan cathedral and the archbishop's palace. On Tuesdays at 11am, don't miss the changing of the guard, a very photogenic ceremony. Sit on a bench, order a fresh fruit juice from a street vendor and watch life unfold around the fountain.

Push open the doors of the Iglesia de la Compañía de Jesús, five minutes away on foot. Built between 1605 and 1765 in gray volcanic stone, its interior covered in gold leaf will leave you speechless—it's the finest example of Baroque art in all of South America. Construction took 160 years, which explains the mix of styles: Mudéjar, Churrigueresque, Neoclassical, and predominantly Baroque. The main altarpiece is considered the crowning achievement of the Quito School of Art. Allow a good hour there.

Continue to Plaza de San Francisco and its immense Franciscan convent, founded as early as 1537 on the ruins of an Inca palace. With 40,000 m² of buildings—thirteen cloisters, three churches—it is nicknamed “the Escorial of the New World”. Inside are over 3,500 colonial artworks and the famous Winged Virgin of Legarda (1734) on the main altar. This is the original whose giant replica stands atop El Panecillo.

In the late afternoon, stroll down Calle La Ronda, the most picturesque pedestrian street in old Quito. Cobblestones, colorful facades, artisan workshops and small cafés line the way. If you're there in the evening, the atmosphere changes: street musicians, open galleries and the scent of canelazo (a hot drink made with cinnamon and aguardiente). A good place to end the day.

If you have time early in the day or in the late afternoon, make a detour to Mitad del Mundo, 25 km north of Quito. The monument marks the equatorial line determined in 1736 by Charles-Marie de La Condamine's expedition. You can put one foot in each hemisphere—the classic photo. Right next door, the Inti Ñan ethnographic museum offers fun experiments on the effects of latitude 0° (water drainage, egg balancing). Allow 1 hour 30 minutes there.

The Basílica del Voto Nacional is visible from everywhere in Quito—the building rises to 115 meters, with towers exceeding 78 m. It's the largest neo-Gothic basilica in the Americas. French architect Emilio Tarlier drew inspiration from Bourges Cathedral when he drafted the plans in 1890, but the cornerstone wasn't laid until 1892, and construction lasted nearly a century. A fun detail: the gargoyles aren't medieval chimeras but iguanas, tortoises, and armadillos—the local wildlife. Quiteños say the day the basilica is finished, the world will end. Climb the towers—bring good shoes, as the final meters involve metal ladders. The view over the historic center is the best in Quito.

Take a taxi to El Panecillo, the hill shaped like a “little bread roll” that rises to 3,016 m. At the top stands the Virgin of Quito, 41 meters including the pedestal, assembled from 7,400 aluminum plates by Spanish sculptor Agustín de la Herrán Matorras and installed in 1976. It is the tallest aluminum statue in the world, taller than Rio's Christ the Redeemer. The 180° view over Quito is superb. Tip: go up by taxi, don't walk up—the neighborhood around the steps is unsafe.

A spectacular climb from Tena to the highlands via the Papallacta road (3–4 hours). You rise from 500 m to over 4,000 m at the pass, then descend to Papallacta at 3,300 m. The landscape changes from stifling jungle to windswept Andean páramo—a striking contrast in just a few hours. Enjoy the panorama of high-altitude lagoons and tall páramo grasses before your stop at the hot springs.

Before continuing to Quito, take the short walk around the Papallacta lagoons in the páramo. The air is pure, the silence total, and the tall grasses ripple in the wind. It's an end-of-the-world landscape at 3,500 m, inhabited by Andean ducks and mountain rabbits. Allow 45 minutes for the loop.

activities.text: A walk through the Rocafuerte neighborhood to try an almuerzo (daily set menu) and encounter traditional herbalists, chocolatiers and restorers of religious statues—a lively side of Quito you won't see in the guidebooks.

Spend the afternoon at the TelefériQo: this cable car takes you in 18 minutes from 3,117 m to 3,947 m above sea level on the slopes of Pichincha volcano—it's one of the highest in the world. From Cruz Loma, the view over Quito is dizzying: the city stretches 40 km long but only 10 km wide. On clear days, you'll see Cotopaxi, Cayambe, and Antisana, all snow-capped. Bring a windbreaker, as it's chilly. If you're well acclimatized, continue on foot toward Rucu Pichincha (4,696 m, 3 hours one way)—the trail is steep and sandy in the final section, but the summit view takes in the entire Avenue of Volcanoes.

Relax in the Papallacta hot springs, Ecuador's most beautiful. Perched at 3,300 m above sea level, the natural hot-water pools (36–40°C) are outdoors, surrounded by mountains and mist. After 10 days of driving, hiking, and altitude, this is the perfect stop to relax your muscles before the return to Quito (1 hour 30 minutes by road).

places.name: Riobamba

visits.text: Spend the day driving along the Avenue of the Volcanoes, this 400 km Andean corridor named by Alexander von Humboldt in 1802. From Quito, you head due south between two rows of volcanoes - Cotopaxi, Tungurahua and Chimborazo appear on the horizon. Stop in Ambato, about 59 km from the overnight city of Riobamba, a 1-hour drive.

About 59 km from Riobamba, a 1-hour drive, Ambato, nicknamed “the city of flowers and fruit”, rarely appears in standard guidebooks but is worth a stop. Founded in the 16th century, it was destroyed three times by earthquakes (1698, 1797, 1949) and rebuilt each time. Walk around Plaza Montalvo and visit the Casa y Mausoleo de Juan Montalvo - this great Ecuadorian writer died in Paris in 1889, and his embalmed body rests in a Greek-style mausoleum. If you pass through on a Monday, the large market fills the streets as Indigenous people from the communities of Pilahuín come down from the mountains to sell their produce.

Arrive in Riobamba in the late afternoon. Perched at 2,750 metres and nicknamed “the Sultana of the Andes”, Riobamba lies at the foot of Chimborazo. Walk around Plaza Maldonado, where the cathedral stands - its façade is one of the few remnants of the original city, founded in 1534 near Colta Lagoon before the 1797 earthquake forced its relocation.

Head towards Chimborazo, about a 1-hour drive from Riobamba. At 6,268 metres, it is Ecuador's highest peak - and, above all, the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre, surpassing Everest because of the equatorial bulge. The road crosses a wildlife reserve covering nearly 60,000 hectares. Keep your eyes open: you will probably see vicuñas, the llama's wild relatives, reintroduced here in the 1990s. They are not timid and raise their heads to watch you curiously - but drive slowly, as they often cross the road.

Drive up to the Hermanos Carrel refuge at 4,800 meters—accessible without special equipment. From there, a trail leads in 40 minutes to the Edward Whymper refuge at 5,000 meters, named after British alpinist Edward Whymper, already famous for conquering the Matterhorn, who reached this summit on January 4, 1880 with the Carrel brothers. At this altitude, every step weighs heavy: go slowly, hydrate constantly. If the sky clears, the glaciated summit appears above you.

activities.text: Head up to Parque 21 de Abril to see Riobamba with Chimborazo as backdrop—the volcano clears more often late in the day than in the morning. Enjoy the evening with some hornado (roast pork), a Sierra specialty. The small restaurants around Mercado La Merced are the most authentic.

On the way back, stop at the community of La Moya (3,200 m). Their Mountain Museum tells the story of the hieleros, men who climbed Chimborazo to fetch blocks of ice to sell at markets. The last known hielero, Baltazar Ushca, practiced this trade alone for decades. His son-in-law hopes to create a memorial trail in his honor. A shared meal with locals will give you a rare glimpse into Andean life.

Active alternative: agencies in Riobamba offer a mountain bike descent from Carrel refuge (4,800 m) down to San Juan village (3,100 m)—33 km and 1,750 meters of descent through the páramo. Duration about 6 hours, accessible without particular experience.

visits.text: From Baños, continue descending toward the Amazon and Puyo (1 hour 30 minutes). You lose more altitude—the heat and humidity increase, and the vegetation becomes dense and tropical. Stop at Mirador Indichuris, 45 minutes south of Puyo: perched at 1,000 m, this viewpoint run by the Indichuris indigenous community (“children of the sun” in Quechua) offers a panoramic view of the confluence of the Puyo and Pastaza rivers and the vast Amazon canopy. There are also caves decorated with carved faces and a swing over the void.

Don't leave without stopping at Paseo de los Monos, a nonprofit refuge deep in the rainforest. Volunteers—sometimes French-speaking—guide you among monkeys, coatis, parrots, and tortoises rescued following seizures from illegal wildlife trafficking. Some animals, too accustomed to humans or with amputated limbs, will never be able to return to the wild. It's a moving place, and the welcome is very warm.

activities.text: A dugout canoe excursion on the Puyo or Napo River to reach an Amazonian Kichwa community. You'll be welcomed with traditional achiote body painting (a red plant pigment), and you can take part in ritual dances and discover how the jungle's medicinal plants are used. It's a short but authentic immersion in the culture of the Oriente peoples.
